statement: Enomoto reports 436 hunting firearms among 955 Shiiba-mountain households in 1745 and 586 firearms in 1836; these are local recorded stocks, not a national ownership rate.

sources.supports: Counts inherited from Fujiki, Katanagari, pp. 168–169.

counterevidence: Household denominator for 1836 is not supplied; recorded ownership may exclude unlicensed guns.
inference_limits: Original village registers not inspected; neither persons armed nor annual use can be calculated.

test.reason: Bounded description of a published local example.

statement: Legal crop-protection and hunting use, together with recorded commoner ownership, contradicts a general account of Tokugawa Japan eliminating guns.

sources.supports: Local firearm records and distinctions among possession, carriage and use.
Common rural firearms and farm-tool uses.
Continued elite and non-elite peacetime niches.

counterevidence: Restrictions and confiscations occurred; persistence does not imply unchanged military effectiveness or unconstrained ownership.
inference_limits: Sources share Japanese historical scholarship; high confidence applies to rejecting total elimination, not to national abundance.

test.reason: Tests a categorical absence claim using positive local evidence; no causal estimate of regulation.

statement: Task-specific permission and peacetime elite appropriation helped accommodate continued firearm use within Tokugawa hierarchies, rather than requiring universal rejection of the technology.

sources.supports: Differentiated regulation and village use.
Licensed commoner use and elite marksmanship/status.

counterevidence: Enforcement weakness or unofficial circulation could also sustain guns; no estimate of their relative weight.
inference_limits: This is a scoped accommodation mechanism, not proof that peace or hierarchy caused a national innovation slowdown.

test.mechanism_chain: Crop/hunting needs and elite interests -> authorities authorize differentiated uses -> firearms retain legitimate niches -> persistence under regulation.
test.strongest_rival: Persistence merely reflects inability to enforce a universal ban.
test.discriminating_observation: Officially acknowledged permissible uses and elite use, not only illicit caches.
test.evidence_sought_found: S01 records authorized local possession; S03 summarizes regulated farming and elite marksmanship.
test.remaining_ambiguity: No matched-domain enforcement comparison; peace, status and livelihood incentives co-evolve.

statement: Howell interprets a shift in Edo-hinterland gun meanings from farm implements toward weapons in the 1840s as responding to anxiety about rural disorder.

sources.supports: Author states the 1840s change and disorder interpretation.

counterevidence: The study might also reflect changing enforcement, reporting vocabulary or later military developments.
inference_limits: Abstract-only access; no independently inspected beliefs, petitions or individual trajectory.

test.mechanism_chain: Perceived disorder -> villagers reinterpret guns as defensive weapons -> social use/meaning changes.
test.strongest_rival: A change in record language or administrative classification rather than in actual behavior.
test.discriminating_observation: Contemporaneous petitions and firing/use records showing changes before external military rearmament.
test.evidence_sought_found: S02 abstract gives the interpretation; underlying examples were unavailable.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Cannot separate behavior, rhetoric and selection from the abstract.

statement: Guan, Palma and Wu distinguish full silver convertibility (1260–76), nominal convertibility (1277–1309) and a fiat regime from 1310; exchange availability and official status were distinct.

sources.supports: Authors reconstruct regime stages and spatially unequal redemption access.

counterevidence: Exact transition boundaries vary by one year in parts of manuscript; local availability could diverge from legal promise.
inference_limits: Periodization is historians’ reconstruction; no uniform household access is inferred.

statement: The study’s reconstructed respectability CPI estimates annual inflation of 11.0% for 1260–1290, 1.8% for 1290–1340 and 4.5% for 1340–1355, contradicting uniform century-long hyperinflation.

sources.supports: Price basket, sparse observations, interpolation, and reported compound rates.

counterevidence: Individual prices and regions differed; the final collapse extends beyond 1355 price data.
inference_limits: About a dozen observations per commodity with interpolation/extrapolation; modelled index, not modern continuous official CPI. No household cost-of-living equivalence.

test.reason: Reports the authors’ bounded calculation and its measurement method.

statement: In the reconstructed 1260–1355 series, civil-war frequency correlates with greater nominal and real note issuance; imperial grants do not show comparable statistical associations in Table 4.

sources.supports: Civil-war coefficients and distinctions among nominal/real issues and rival demands.

counterevidence: Natural disasters weakly correlate with real issuance at the 10% level; external-war coefficients are not significant.
inference_limits: Political disorder, inflation and fiscal erosion can reinforce each other. No exogenous shock identifies the fiscal channel; absence of significance is not proof of no effect.

test.mechanism_chain: Civil conflict -> fiscal demands/tax difficulty -> greater note issuance -> potential pressure on currency value.
test.strongest_rival: Inflation and collapsing revenue cause civil conflict; or imperial grants/disasters dominate spending.
test.discriminating_observation: Different associations for war types and grants, with temporally ordered independently measured fiscal shortages.
test.evidence_sought_found: S04 Table 4 finds civil-war associations in nominal/real issues, no grant association, and weak real-disaster associations; only sparse fiscal totals.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Annual reconstructed time series does not remove reciprocal causation or omitted political changes; fiscal intermediate evidence incomplete.

statement: Yuan legal monetary unification coexisted with regional and task-specific practices: Ichimaru reports different uses of guanwen and dingliang, while Guan et al. report silver property transactions despite official restrictions.

sources.supports: Regional account-unit and government/commercial distinctions.
Private silver use and Yunnan cowry exception.

counterevidence: A regional unit of account is not automatically a different circulating medium.
inference_limits: Contract-level evidence in S05 not inspected; formal legal-tender scope must not be equated with every transaction.

test.reason: Separates observable institutional rules, units of account and reported practices.

statement: Polo’s paper-money narrative combines threat of punishment for refusal with portability, official authentication and damaged-note replacement; it cannot independently establish willing universal acceptance.

sources.supports: Narrative explicitly juxtaposes coercion and convenient transactions/redemption.

counterevidence: The narrative also insists on ready acceptance and enormous imperial riches; these are claims to assess, not measured outcomes.
inference_limits: Confidence is high about text content; the frequency of punishments, distribution of consent and national coverage are unknown.

test.reason: Source-critical description, not validation of every traveler assertion.

statement: Late-Qing telegraph development included strategic state priorities and controlled private operation; the Gao–Lei sample records office access for 64 of 130 rice-reporting prefectures by 1904.

sources.locator: pp. 7–9 and 12–13, sections I.A and II.B
sources.supports: Strategic line-building narrative; explicit sample treatment counts.

counterevidence: Routes could still reflect economic geography; state priorities do not prove random placement.
inference_limits: Sample is nine provinces, not all Qing territory; office presence does not measure affordability, uptime or individual usage.

statement: Yoon argues that shareholder-dividend priorities, underinvestment, high charges and technical/service problems limited the telegraph’s popular use even after network establishment.

sources.supports: Author links shareholder returns, equipment choices, pricing and limited market reach.

counterevidence: Gao–Lei find price effects consistent with commercially useful communication; limited mass use is compatible with gains among traders.
inference_limits: Abstract-only; no audited tariff-demand series or proof that dividends, rather than scarce capital/risk, caused underinvestment.

test.mechanism_chain: Dividend demands -> constrained equipment investment/high fees -> unreliable expensive service -> restricted public uptake.
test.strongest_rival: High capital costs, risk or low demand require high tariffs; technical failures precede rather than result from financing choices.
test.discriminating_observation: Investment decisions and dividend commitments preceding delays, with comparable capital-cost routes or customer elasticities.
test.evidence_sought_found: S08 abstract supplies mechanism; full budgets and customer series unavailable. S07 finds beneficial price effects on a different margin.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Cannot choose among financing and demand mechanisms; do not generalize to all state/private ownership models.

statement: Zhou and Ding portray Sheng Xuanhuai as defending telegraph investors against court encroachment while also having entangled personal interests; the abstract records a proposal for state purchase instead of appropriation.

sources.supports: Conflicted official/investor interests and purchase-versus-confiscation proposal.

counterevidence: The Chinese abstract also notes Sheng sometimes pressured shareholders from the court’s side.
inference_limits: A proposal is not completed reform, public consultation or popular legitimacy; underlying correspondence not inspected.

test.reason: Attributed description of actors and proposals, not a causal claim of modernization.

statement: Gao and Lei’s difference-in-differences study estimates that telegraph office access reduced monthly maximum high-quality rice prices by about 4.2–5.5% of the sample mean in 130 prefectures over 1870–1904.

sources.supports: Data, specifications, effect magnitudes and pretrend checks.

counterevidence: Office placement was not randomized; reporting changes and time-varying conflicts could remain. Lower-quality rice estimates are smaller/less precise.
inference_limits: Outcome is reported monthly wholesale maxima, not average consumer expenditure, famine deaths or welfare; original regressions not replicated.

test.mechanism_chain: Faster information across existing trade routes -> merchants adjust orders -> lower local price extremes.
test.strongest_rival: Coincident transport/institutional change, placement selection or altered reporting accounts for falling maxima.
test.discriminating_observation: Pretrends, transport/port controls, route/subsample tests and reactions to connected versus unconnected external shocks.
test.evidence_sought_found: S07 checks pretrends, railway/treaty-port controls, excludes selected locations and tests weather/network channels.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Assumed June treatment month, spillovers, official reporting quality and staggered-treatment assumptions remain; no household outcomes.

statement: The same study finds telegraph access dampened local-weather price effects but increased sensitivity to weather in connected regions; price volatility rose in previously stable markets and fell in previously volatile ones.

sources.supports: Weather-location interactions, disconnected-region placebo and volatility heterogeneity.

counterevidence: The result is shared-risk transmission, not uniform stabilization; estimated mechanisms depend on exposure weights and reported weather.
inference_limits: Same sample as K13, not independent corroboration; no distribution of gains among net buyers, sellers or laborers.

test.mechanism_chain: Connected price information -> trade arbitrage links markets -> local shocks spread -> less local isolation and redistributed risk.
test.strongest_rival: General administrative change reduces price volatility everywhere regardless of network.
test.discriminating_observation: Opposite responses to local and connected distant shocks; no similar response to disconnected shocks.
test.evidence_sought_found: S07 reports these directional tests and heterogeneous volatility by baseline risk.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Trade flows and household welfare not directly measured; weight/model choices and common reporting may matter.

statement: The 1812 imperial decree retained metric base units while ordering commercially familiar fractions/multiples and dual markings on instruments, and retained official metric teaching.

sources.supports: Direct decree on unchanged units, adapted instruments and teaching.
Retail implementation and legal continuity.

counterevidence: The resulting arrangements modified decimal practice; describing unchanged base units alone would hide a substantial compromise.
inference_limits: Law states what was authorized and intended, not how widely instruments were supplied or accepted.

test.reason: Direct legal configuration, carefully distinguished from compliance.

statement: A material implementation gap accompanied early metric mandates: Treat reports that secondary standards had not been distributed when compulsory use was declared in 1795.

sources.supports: Secondary standards/commercial instrument shortfall.
Municipal standard provision and later conversion tables.

counterevidence: Familiarity, pricing interests and political disruption also constrained uptake; instruments alone would not ensure adoption.
inference_limits: Retrospective evidence does not estimate what share of delay was caused by supply constraints.

test.mechanism_chain: Mandate before local standards/instruments -> users lack calibrated practical implements -> legal uniformity fails to ensure comparable practice.
test.strongest_rival: Users had sufficient implements but deliberately resisted new measures.
test.discriminating_observation: Dated deliveries/orders compared with local compliance, including places supplied early.
test.evidence_sought_found: S13 states missing secondary standards; S12 describes municipal supply and tables. No matched delivery/compliance panel inspected.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Physical and social obstacles could operate together; relative contributions unmeasured.

statement: The law of 4 July 1837 repealed the 1812 arrangement and prohibited nonmetric measures from 1 January 1840; this supplies a legal deadline, not a date of universal practical adoption.

sources.supports: Repeal and effective date.
Translated prohibitions including commercial/legal settings.

counterevidence: Older words and task measures persisted according to the Isère synthesis.
inference_limits: Both accounts derive from the same law; original Bulletin des lois not inspected. No national compliance denominator.

test.reason: Corroborated legal sequence; explicit non-equivalence to use.

statement: The Isère archival synthesis describes customary measures tied to agricultural work and continued rural usage beyond the 1840 legal deadline; practical task fit is a plausible part of persistence, not a measured universal preference.

sources.locator: PDF pp. 2, 6–9, especially journal/land-work discussion and long-run coda
sources.supports: Task-linked area measures, local implementation and later coexistence.

counterevidence: Habit, limited schooling, fraud and political resistance may also explain use; the source does not isolate these channels.
inference_limits: Coda extends beyond 1795–1840 and is used only to reject instantaneous displacement. Neither continued terminology nor local examples establish unchanged quantities nationally.

test.mechanism_chain: Established work/commodity conventions -> customary units remain useful for local tasks -> continued mixed practice despite a legal standard.
test.strongest_rival: Pure inertia or educational exclusion, with no continuing practical utility.
test.discriminating_observation: Contexts where a task-linked measure persists as the task persists and changes when work changes, despite ability to use metric units.
test.evidence_sought_found: S12 links the journal to horse-ploughing and describes later rural coexistence; no individual longitudinal literacy/use evidence.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Source offers qualitative association, not a discriminating controlled comparison.
